title: The unmarked fuse box
text: A client's fuse box has no labels at all, three decades of someone else's improvisation, and a smell like warm pennies.

choices.label: Map every circuit before touching it

outcomes.text: Two hours of patient tracing. I found a wire that would have killed the next person. I left a laminated map on the door.
It took until midnight, and the client grumbled about the hours. The map hung there for years.

choices.label: Isolate at the mains and work fast

outcomes.text: Safe, quick, tidy. The client was grateful and gave me a bottle of whisky.
I missed one live neutral. The tingle in my arm told me everything.

choices.label: Tell the client it needs a full rewire

outcomes.text: It did. They were upset, but they listened, and I got a good job out of it.
They called someone cheaper who patched it. I heard it burned out a year later.

title: The storm callout
text: At 11 p.m. a lightning strike has taken out the street. A frantic woman tells you her elderly father is on an oxygen machine and the power's been out an hour.

outcomes.text: It was a tripped main. Thirty seconds of work and a lot of relief. She hugged me on the doorstep.
Half the street's lines were down. I rigged a generator for him and stayed until it was fixed.

choices.label: Tell her to call the emergency service

outcomes.text: They dispatched a crew. Quicker than I'd have been, in all honesty.
They took three hours. She never rang me again.

choices.label: Go, but charge the emergency rate

outcomes.text: Fair, within the rate card. She paid without argument.
She paid and then wrote a review about 'profiteering'. It stung.

title: The ceiling stain
text: A woman rings in a panic: the ceiling below her bathroom is bulging, brown and glistening. 'It's not just water,' she says darkly.

choices.label: Go straight up and find the leak

outcomes.text: A cracked soil pipe. A grim hour and a fix that held. I could smell victory, and the other thing.
It was the pipe, and the wall behind, and the floor joist. A bigger job than anyone hoped.

choices.label: Cut the water first, then look

outcomes.text: The right order of things. Nobody drowned.
I cut the wrong stopcock. The neighbour called, upset about her shower.

choices.label: Give a quote over the phone

outcomes.text: I was close enough. The customer thought I was a wizard.
I was wildly off. The final invoice was twice the quote.

title: The wedding ring
text: A tearful customer says she dropped her late mother's ring down the sink. 'If you can get it back...' She holds out an envelope.

outcomes.text: It was in the U-bend, glinting. She cried and I pretended not to.
It was in the main drain. Three hours of digging in the rain. We found it.
She paid. It was fair, and she knew it.
She declined, and left it. I felt awful all week.

choices.label: Say it's gone, to save the effort

outcomes.text: She believed me. I knew I'd lied. It sat with me.
She asked another plumber, who found it in minutes. She told everyone.

title: The knock that isn't
text: A man insists his engine has a knock. You listen for twenty minutes and hear nothing. He is certain, and growing certain you are lying.

choices.label: Take it on a road test

outcomes.text: A loose heat shield, rattling at 40 mph only. I tightened a bolt. He paid me in disbelief.
Nothing at all. I told him it was fine. He seemed disappointed.
He agreed. I did not feel good about that sale.
He went elsewhere. Good.

choices.label: Tell him honestly there's nothing wrong

outcomes.text: He argued for ten minutes and then, sheepish, said thanks. A rare honest customer.
He left angry and told everyone I was useless.

title: A very fast customer
text: A shiny sports car rolls in with a faint pull to the left and an owner with no patience. 'Fix it by five.' It is a quarter to.

outcomes.text: I did it right. He was furious at the lateness and then delighted at the drive home.
He left a one-star review for the delay. The boss backed me.
It was fine. He was thrilled. I breathed out.
A bolt came loose on the motorway. He was fine. He sued.

choices.label: Tell him to come back tomorrow

outcomes.text: He blustered and agreed. He was nicer when he came back.
He took it to a rival garage. We lost him.

title: Measure twice
text: You've cut the final beam for a client's loft staircase and it is a full two centimetres too short. The client arrives in an hour.

outcomes.text: I told him. He sighed and said 'that happens'. It cost an extra day and a lot of respect.
He laughed so hard he cried. We bonded over my mistake.
It held. He never noticed. Neither did the building inspector.
It sagged within a year and I got a call.
A lovely quirk. The client said it had 'character' and paid extra.
The result was odd, and the client was too polite to say so.

title: Something in the wall
text: Behind a bookshelf you're removing in a 1920s house you find a small door, a hollow, and a tin box wrapped in an old newspaper from the war.

outcomes.text: Letters, a medal, and a photograph of a young man. The owner didn't speak for a while.
A handful of coins and a note. The owner was delighted. We went for tea.
Old coins, mostly. I resealed it and told the owner. I felt cheap for looking.
I found something I wasn't meant to see. I left it where it was.

choices.label: Leave it sealed and say nothing

outcomes.text: I thought about it for years.
The next carpenter found it. He kept it.

title: The bad cut
text: You've taken a centimetre too much and the client, mid-chat, hasn't noticed yet. In ten seconds she will look at the mirror.

outcomes.text: She laughed, then fixed her face and asked for a 'bold choice'. It was a hit.
She cried, then forgave me. The salon gave her a free treatment.

choices.label: Style it so it looks intended

outcomes.text: A little product, a few clever cuts, and she left delighted.
She noticed within a day and was cool about it. She never came back.
She bought it. She told her friends. It became one.
Her friends laughed. She never forgave me.

title: The confession chair
text: A regular, mid-wash, tells you she is leaving her husband tonight. 'I haven't told anyone yet. I just needed to say it somewhere safe.'

outcomes.text: I cut her hair slowly and said nothing. She hugged me on the way out.
She cried softly into the towel. I kept the chair warm for her the next week.
I told her she deserved better. She took it as permission.
She told me to mind my business. I did.
It was awkward. She was gone in half an hour.
I told her about my dog. She laughed through tears. It was the right thing.

title: Slammed on a Saturday
text: The ticket printer won't stop. Twenty-one covers on the pass, the sous-chef out sick, and the head chef staring at you like a hawk.

choices.label: Take the grill and the sauté together

outcomes.text: I became a machine. The ticket rail went clear for the first time that night. The chef nodded once, and that was enough.
I burnt a steak and plated it anyway. A customer noticed.

choices.label: Call it out and ask for help

outcomes.text: The pastry chef jumped in. We got through it as a team.
The chef barked. I got the help, and a reputation as someone who panics.

choices.label: Go slow and get it right

outcomes.text: Dishes went out late, but perfect. Two covers walked, the rest raved.
The chef pulled me off the line. I washed pots.

title: The staff meal
text: At the end of a long night, the head chef shoves a pan at you: 'Make staff meal. Surprise me.' Everyone is watching.

outcomes.text: Everyone went silent, then asked for seconds. The chef asked for the recipe.
It was good, in a way that made me homesick.
The room cheered. The chef raised an eyebrow, then took a bite and sighed.
It was overcooked. The chef said nothing, which was the worst.
Pasta is never wrong. Everyone ate and fell asleep.
Pasta again. The chef rolled his eyes. It was fine.

title: The call at 4 a.m.
text: The tones drop and your boots are on before you're awake. A warehouse fire, with a woman on the third floor, screaming from a window.

outcomes.text: I got her down. She was singed but fine. They gave me a commendation I didn't know what to do with.
I got her out, but the floor behind us caved. I'll never forget the sound.
It arrived in ninety seconds and she was out. That was the textbook. I didn't feel good about the wait.
She didn't wait. She jumped. She survived, barely.
Nobody was in it. Good thing. Every second counts.
I found a second person. We got them both out.

title: Cat in the tree, again
text: The dispatcher says, with real feeling, 'It's a cat. In a tree.' The whole station stares into their coffee.

outcomes.text: I climbed twelve feet with a blanket and a bag of treats. A child cried with joy. The cat bit me.
It came down on its own while I was reaching. The child gave me a drawing.
The rookie got scratched to ribbons. The crew laughed for a week.
He got it, to a round of applause. His first rescue.
I told them to call a cat rescue service. The dispatcher sighed.
The cat was fine. It came down by tea time.

title: The dog on route 14
text: House number nine has a dog that has been eyeing you for three weeks. Today the gate is open.

outcomes.text: The dog sniffed my boots and went home. A truce.
The dog bit my satchel and tugged it away. I fought for a minute and won.
A friend for life. He waited by the gate every morning after.
He took it and bit me anyway.
I delivered it the next day, apologetic, to a furious owner.
The owner never found out. I smiled all the way to number ten.

title: A letter, thirty years late
text: In a sorting-room crate you find a handwritten letter, postmarked three decades ago, never delivered, addressed to a woman at an address on your route.

outcomes.text: She opened it on the doorstep and read it in silence. She said it was from her brother. She hugged me for a minute.
She'd moved. I tracked her down through three neighbours. It took a month. It was worth it.
It went into a drawer, and I never found out what happened.
They sent it on officially. A form letter replaced the story.
I read it. I shouldn't have. I put it back in the post, years late.
I kept it in a drawer for a long time.

title: Turbulence
text: The seatbelt sign dings and the cabin begins to jump. A child is crying, a man is gripping his armrest, and you're standing in the aisle with a cart.

choices.label: Strap in and talk to the child

outcomes.text: I told a story about a plane that sneezes. She giggled. The turbulence ended. The mother cried.
It worked until the next bump. Then she was sick on my shoe.

choices.label: Calm the cabin over the intercom

outcomes.text: My voice was steadier than I felt. The cabin settled.
My voice cracked. Half the plane saw.
It ended in ninety seconds. I was fine.
It lasted twenty minutes. I was not fine.

title: The passenger in 14C
text: Mid-flight, a man in 14C is clearly unwell: pale, sweating, hand clutched to his chest. 'Is there a doctor on board?'

outcomes.text: A doctor appeared. We worked together and he survived. I got a letter from the airline.
The plane diverted. He lived. I cried in the galley.

choices.label: Call the captain and make him comfortable

outcomes.text: It was just indigestion, in the end. He was embarrassed.
It was a heart attack. The crew's quick work saved him.
Another crew member took charge. I learned something about myself.
I blinked, and then I moved. The training had stuck.

title: Friday deploy
text: It's 4:55 on a Friday and someone has pushed a change to production. The error rate graph has started to climb, slowly and then not slowly.

outcomes.text: A one-line revert, and the graph came back down. The team clapped sarcastically. I loved them.
The rollback broke something else. I was online until 2 a.m.
A quick patch, a prayer, and it worked. I felt like a god.
The patch made things worse. I rolled back at midnight, humbled.
Someone else fixed it. I went home and had a drink.
It was my change. They found out. I have never lived it down.

title: The bug nobody can reproduce
text: Users report a crash. The logs are empty, the tests pass, and you've spent three days trying to make it happen on your own machine.

outcomes.text: Day four, 2 a.m.: a leap-year bug. I laughed out loud alone. Best feeling in the world.
Day six: a timezone bug. I sent a thank-you to nobody.
She saw it in three minutes. I swallowed my pride.
She said, 'oh, that.' She'd seen it before. We fixed it together.
It came back in a week, bigger. I looked foolish.
It never came back. Sometimes the universe is kind.

title: Crunch week
text: The release date is in nine days and the build has eleven blockers. The producer has started saying 'we all believe in this team' a lot.

outcomes.text: We shipped on time. I slept for 14 hours and woke up to good reviews.
We shipped on time, and my relationship barely survived it.
We lost two features and kept our sanity. Reviews were kind.
We cut the wrong feature. Players noticed.
The studio delayed, and the game was better for it.
The publisher pulled funding. It was an awful month.

title: The playtest
text: A stranger sits down in the playtest room to try your level. Within ninety seconds they've done the one thing you were certain no one would.

outcomes.text: A flaw I'd never have seen. We fixed it, and the level got better.
They loved it. They broke it. They loved that, too.
The tester was kind, I was not. I regretted it.
I was wrong. It was embarrassing.

choices.label: Quietly fix the bug and move on

outcomes.text: Nobody ever knew. I slept well.
It broke again two weeks later. I fixed it again.

title: The patient who won't take the pill
text: An elderly man refuses his medication, calmly and entirely. 'I'm eighty-four. I'd like to choose.' The ward is busy and there are forty minutes of paperwork behind the pill.

outcomes.text: He had been a sailor. Pills made him feel 'like a boat tied up forever'. We found a compromise.
He told me a lot about his wife and I lost track of time. A matron raised an eyebrow, then smiled.
The doctor sat with him and agreed to adjust the regimen. A good outcome.
The doctor sighed and ordered the pill anyway. I felt complicit.
It was within policy, and he was fine. I was fine.
He deteriorated overnight. I replayed that conversation for weeks.

title: Night shift, short-staffed
text: Two nurses off sick, twenty-six patients and one call bell that will not stop. At 3 a.m. you realise you haven't sat down since seven.

outcomes.text: We held the ward. By morning I could barely speak, and I was proud.
I missed a dose. It was caught. I cried in the sluice room.
A float nurse arrived and we all breathed again.
None was available. I was told so quietly.
I did the sick first and the grumpy last. Nobody died, and the grumpy forgave me.
A complaint came in about the grumpy. It was fair, and also not.

title: The disruptive back row
text: Two students in the back are whispering through your entire lesson. You've asked twice. You can feel the whole class waiting.

outcomes.text: It took forty seconds. The room went still. The two blushed and stopped. It's an old trick, and it works.
They kept talking. The class started giggling. I lost the room.
Quiet efficiency. The lesson resumed.
One of them turned out to be explaining the work to the other. I felt rotten.

choices.label: Ask them to share with the class

outcomes.text: They'd been discussing the topic. Better than my lesson. We spent the hour on it.
They'd been discussing a video game. The class loved it. I did not.

title: The marking pile
text: It is Sunday night and there are sixty essays in a bag by the door. One of them has a note on the first page: 'I know it's bad, please be kind.'

outcomes.text: It was brave and flawed. I wrote a long comment. She came to see me, and I think it changed something.
It was exactly as she said. I was kind. She cried in the corridor, in a good way.

choices.label: Mark it all in one go

outcomes.text: I stayed up until two. Efficient and exhausted, I fell asleep in a staff meeting.
Quality dropped around essay forty. I knew it.

choices.label: Give them all the same mark

outcomes.text: Nobody noticed. I never felt right about it.
A parent noticed. I got called in.

title: A routine stop
text: You pull over a car for a broken tail light. The driver is shaking, polite, and keeps glancing at the passenger seat, where a bag sits very still.

outcomes.text: A birthday cake, from a shop that had closed. A tearful, comic scene. I let him go.
Something that shouldn't have been there. An arrest, a long night, and a good result.

choices.label: Write the ticket and move on

outcomes.text: Quick, uneventful, and by the book.
I found out later what was in the bag. I couldn't forgive myself.
It was a long wait for nothing, but that's the job.
Backup arrived just as the driver bolted. We got him.

title: The lost child
text: A four-year-old is found alone at midnight, in pyjamas, outside a closed shop, holding a toy rabbit and giving a very firm name for his mother.

choices.label: Sit with him until his mum is found

outcomes.text: Three hours later a woman came sprinting down the road. She had fallen asleep on the sofa and he'd wandered. She sobbed. I gave her the rabbit.
It was a long night, and an even longer talk with social services. But he was safe.

choices.label: Take him straight to the station

outcomes.text: A warm blanket, a biscuit, and a very good night's work.
He fell asleep in the car and I drove with the window cracked open to keep myself awake.
Dispatch found his family in ten minutes. I spent the rest of the shift thinking about it.
Nothing for an hour. The longest hour.
